books.section: Great Depression and the New Deal (1929-1939)

primary_sources: Paraphrase of President Theodore Roosevelt's "New Nationalism" speech, August 31, 1910
Paraphrase of the Espionage Act, June 1917
Paraphrase of the National Origins Act, 1924
Paraphrase of the Social Security Act, August 1935
Description of the Works Progress Administration poster "Work Pays America!" (1937)

source: original; documents drawn from paraphrases of 1910-1942 laws, orders, and speeches, and a description of a 1937 government poster
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the federal government's role in American society and the economy changed from 1900 to 1945.

documents.title: The New Nationalism
documents.source: Paraphrase of President Theodore Roosevelt's "New Nationalism" speech, Osawatomie, Kansas, August 31, 1910.
documents.text: Paraphrase: Roosevelt said the executive power should act as the steward of the public welfare, and that government should serve human welfare rather than property and represent all the people rather than any one class.
documents.sourcing: A campaign speech by a former president setting out a reform program. It states an aim, not a law already passed.

documents.title: New tools for Washington
documents.source: Paraphrase of the Sixteenth Amendment and the Federal Reserve Act, both 1913, as described in Barron's Chapter 9.
documents.text: Paraphrase: In 1913 the Sixteenth Amendment gave Congress power to tax incomes, and the Federal Reserve Act created a central banking system to control credit and stabilize the money supply. For the first time the federal government had both a broad revenue base and a central bank.
documents.sourcing: Two 1913 measures described together. They gave Washington permanent tools, not just a one-time response to a crisis.

documents.title: The Espionage Act
documents.source: Paraphrase of the Espionage Act, June 1917.
documents.text: Paraphrase: The act made it a crime to interfere with military recruiting or to speak against the war effort. The government jailed critics, including the Socialist leader Eugene V. Debs, and in Schenck v. United States (1919) the Supreme Court upheld the convictions.
documents.sourcing: A wartime law. Students should weigh its claim of military necessity against its effect on speech.

documents.title: The National Origins Act
documents.source: Paraphrase of the National Origins Act, 1924.
documents.text: Paraphrase: The act set yearly quotas for immigrants at 2 percent of each nationality's population in the United States in 1890, a formula that favored northern and western Europeans. It barred immigration from Asia almost entirely.
documents.sourcing: A law that used federal power to choose who could enter the country. It shows Washington managing the population, not only the economy.

documents.title: The Social Security Act
documents.source: Paraphrase of the Social Security Act, August 1935.
documents.text: Paraphrase: The act created old-age pensions for retired workers, unemployment insurance, and aid for dependent children, paid for by taxes on workers and employers. Farm and domestic workers, many of them Black and Latino, were left out of the pension system.
documents.sourcing: A New Deal law that made the federal government a permanent provider of income security. Its exclusions show the limits of that promise.

documents.title: Work Pays America!
documents.source: Description of the Works Progress Administration poster "Work Pays America!" (1937), Federal Art Project.
documents.text: Description: The poster shows a strong worker holding a shovel, with the words "Work Pays America!" across the top. The poster was one of thousands printed by the Federal Art Project to advertise government jobs programs.
documents.sourcing: A government poster advertising its own jobs program. It shows Washington presenting itself as an employer, not only a regulator.

documents.title: Executive Order 9066
documents.text: Paraphrase: President Roosevelt ordered the removal of about 120,000 Japanese Americans, most of them citizens, from the West Coast to camps in the interior. In Korematsu v. United States (1944) the Supreme Court upheld the order as a wartime necessity.
documents.sourcing: A wartime order by the president alone, without a vote of Congress. Students should weigh its wartime setting against the rights of citizens.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the federal government's role in American society and the economy changed from 1900 to 1945, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the Gilded Age's weak federal government, the Progressive Era's reform movement, or the two world wars that expanded Washington's power.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument, or background from a later century, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument.
rubric.notEarned: Naming documents without describing their content does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or describing them without tying them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the Wagner Act of 1935, the Tennessee Valley Authority, the War Production Board, or the Manhattan Project.
rubric.notEarned: A vague reference to the New Deal or the war with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation, such as a reform speech stating an aim rather than a law, a wartime law limiting speech, or a government poster advertising its own program.
rubric.notEarned: Naming an author without explaining why the authorship matters does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for showing a complex understanding, such as explaining that the federal role grew in both war and peace but left racial exclusion largely intact, or weighing change against continuity across the documents.
rubric.notEarned: A one-sided argument that treats the period as only change or only continuity does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: the federal government's role changed to a great extent between 1900 and 1945, growing from a referee over business into a provider of income security and a director of the wartime economy, though the growth was uneven and left racial exclusion largely intact.

Group 1, new tools and aims: Documents 1 and 2, the New Nationalism speech and the 1913 measures, show Washington gaining both a reform aim and permanent tools, the income tax and the central bank.
Group 2, war and population: Documents 3, 4, and 7, the Espionage Act, the National Origins Act, and Executive Order 9066, show Washington using its power over speech, immigration, and citizens themselves.
Group 3, the New Deal turn: Documents 5 and 6, the Social Security Act and the WPA poster, show Washington becoming an employer and a provider of income security.

Outside evidence: the Wagner Act of 1935, the Tennessee Valley Authority, and the War Production Board. Complexity: the same growth that built a safety net also built the power to jail critics and intern citizens, and the safety net excluded many Black and Latino workers, so change and limits came together.
